title: The roles of three probe types

opening.headline: It explains why, during model loading, the liveness probe fails and the pod keeps restarting, by differentiating the roles of the three probes.
body: There is a container that takes several minutes to load a model. After attaching a liveness probe to this container, the probe fails before the loading is complete, causing the pod to continuously restart. Each time the pod restarts, the model is reloaded from the beginning, resulting in a vicious cycle.

In this lesson, we examine what each of startup, readiness, and liveness probes determines and what changes occur when they fail. We gain an understanding of how readiness and traffic forwarding are connected, and learn the criteria for evaluating whether probe configurations are appropriate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of startup, readiness, and liveness probes
You can distinguish between ready state and traffic forwarding.
Can determine whether the probe configuration is appropriate for the service

screens.title: Live failure occurs during model loading, causing repeated restarts.
screens.lead: This is a common vicious cycle in model services. You can verify what the issue is by selecting each item.

visual.alt: A circular loop where a liveness probe fails before model loading is complete, causing repeated restarts.
labels: Container starting · model loading in progress

items.prompt: There is a container that takes several minutes to load the model.
items.answer: The service is not ready simply because the container process has started. The model server does not respond to requests while it is reading files and loading them into memory. How this initialization phase is handled is the starting point of this course.

items.prompt: The liveness probe fails during loading, causing the container to continuously restart.
items.answer: A liveness probe determines whether a container is in a state that requires a restart. If a container that is loading fails to respond, the probe is considered failed, and if the number of allowed failures is exceeded, kubelet will restart the container.

items.prompt: Each restart creates a vicious cycle of reloading the model from scratch.
items.answer: A restarted container begins loading from the start again, and the probe fails once more before the loading process completes. This effectively prevents the desired device from ever being ready for service.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: what does each probe assess and what does it modify?

screens.title: Preview: probe three
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: Can you explain the difference among the three probes?
items.answer: These three probes are all diagnostic checks periodically sent by kubelet to containers, but they ask different questions. Startup checks whether the pod has completed its startup, liveness checks whether a restart is needed, and readiness checks whether the container is ready to receive traffic.

items.prompt: What does each kubelet do when it fails?
items.answer: If startup or liveness probes fail, kubelet kills or restarts the container; if readiness probes fail, the container remains running but is excluded from the service's endpoints. The key point is that the outcomes differ.

items.prompt: Can the same signal be used to indicate both the fact that the service is not yet ready and the fact that the service has died?
items.answer: This should not be handled. Unprepared containers should be waited for, and dead containers should be restarted. If both situations are treated with the same signal, a problem arises where restarts occur when waiting is actually required.

screens.outro: Let's compare the roles of each of the three probes one by one.

screens.title: Roles of startup, liveness, and readiness
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the three probes determine whether something fails and what happens when a failure occurs.

visual.alt: A timeline diagram showing the intervals during which startup, liveness, and readiness probes are executed throughout a container's lifecycle.

tabs.label: startup probe
tabs.body:
The startup probe checks whether the application inside the container has started. If configured, liveness and readiness probes are not executed until success is achieved, giving the application time to complete its initialization.

This probe runs only at startup. If it fails, kubelet terminates the container, and the container follows its restart policy. It is designed for containers that take a long time to start.

tabs.label: liveness probe
tabs.body:
A liveness probe determines when a container should be restarted. A typical use case is detecting a deadlocked state where the application appears to be running but is no longer making progress. If the number of failures exceeds the allowed threshold, kubelet will restart the container.

This probe must be used with care. It should be configured to indicate only irrecoverable failures, and improper usage may lead to a chain of failures where containers restart under high load, causing increased workload on remaining pods.

tabs.label: readiness probe
tabs.body:
A readiness probe determines whether a container is ready to receive traffic. It is useful when waiting for time-consuming initial operations such as establishing network connections, reading files, or warming up caches.

If the probe fails, the EndpointSlice controller removes the pod's IP address from the service's endpoints; if it succeeds again, the IP is restored. The container is not restarted. Since this probe runs throughout the container's lifecycle, it can be used during recovery from temporary overloads or outages.

tabs.label: When something occurs
tabs.body:
If a container typically takes longer than `initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold × periodSeconds` to start up, configure a startup probe. This means waiting separately for the container to start, rather than increasing the liveness probe interval.

If a process terminates due to self-failure, a liveness probe is not strictly necessary. If you only want to receive traffic after the service is ready, configure a readiness probe. With a readiness probe in place, the pod starts without traffic and begins receiving traffic only after the probe succeeds.

screens.outro: I will read you the scenario of setting three probes together in one pod.

screens.title: Set three probes in one container
screens.lead: Probe configuration for the model server container. Check the meaning by line number and symptoms when misaligned in the right-side description.

data.code:
containers:
- name: server
  image: example/model-server:1.0
  ports:
  - name: liveness-port
    containerPort: 8080
  startupProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /healthz
      port: liveness-port
    failureThreshold: 30
    periodSeconds: 10
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /healthz
      port: liveness-port
    periodSeconds: 10
  readinessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /ready
      port: liveness-port
    periodSeconds: 5

notes.note: Attach the name liveness-port to the container port. The following probes refer to this port by this name; if the port name differs, the probes will fail to locate the target and will continue to fail.

The startupProbe has kubelet send an HTTP GET request to /healthz to check if the request is successful (an exec method is also available). With failureThreshold set to 30 and periodSeconds set to 10, kubelet waits up to 300 seconds for the startup to complete. If a successful response is received at any point during this time, the liveness probe is considered successful and continues; if all attempts fail, kubelet terminates the container and applies the restart policy. The symptom is repeated restarts.

The livenessProbe runs only after the startup is successful. Since the same /healthz endpoint is used, startup readiness and deadlocking detection can be separated using different thresholds. If initialDelaySeconds and periodSeconds are set shorter than the model loading time, the liveness probe will fail first without a startup phase.

The readinessProbe checks whether the pod is ready to receive traffic by listening on the /ready endpoint. Pods that have not yet succeeded remain absent from the service endpoint and thus do not receive traffic; if execution fails, the endpoint removes the pod, and upon recovery, it is restored. Without this probe, the container begins receiving traffic immediately upon startup, resulting in failed loading requests.

screens.outro: Now let's directly diagnose a case where the settings are inappropriate.

screens.title: Explanation: Why a startup probe is needed for a service with long model loading time
screens.lead: The instructor finds and fixes the cause of repeated restarts in a service configured with only a liveness probe. Please follow along by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: A timeline bar chart comparing the point when liveness determines a restart and the point when model loading completes.

steps.title: Read setting
steps.body: This service only has `livenessProbe` and does not have `startupProbe`. The probe sends an HTTP GET request via `/healthz` and checks against `initialDelaySeconds: 5`, `periodSeconds: 5`, and `failureThreshold: 3`. The symptom is that the pod fails to become ready and only the restart count increases.

steps.title: Step 1: Calculate the allowable time
steps.body: Liveness checks take 5 + 3 × 5 = 20 seconds to determine a restart. The container begins checking every 5 seconds starting after 5 seconds of startup, and a restart occurs if three consecutive checks fail. However, the model loading for this service takes significantly longer than 20 seconds. The liveness probe fails before the loading is complete, which is the root cause.

steps.title: Stage 2: Drawbacks that arise simply by increasing the gap
steps.body: The initial latency and period of liveness could be increased to address the issue. However, this value is still used for deadlock detection after the transition has completed, thereby delaying the detection. Since movement waiting and deadlock detection serve different purposes, it is difficult to configure them with a single setting.

steps.title: Step 3: Add a startup probe
steps.body: Add `startupProbe` to check endpoints such as liveness, along with `failureThreshold: 30` and `periodSeconds: 10`. Wait up to 300 seconds for startup, and if successful, liveness is inherited. The default value of liveness is left unchanged to maintain rapid detection of deadlocks.

steps.title: Step 4: Block traffic with readiness and keep liveness lightweight
steps.body: Set `readinessProbe` to prevent traffic during model loading. Configure liveness with a lightweight endpoint check and a generous threshold to avoid cascading restarts due to temporary overload. If the startup time exceeds 300 seconds, increase `failureThreshold`. By dividing the three probes among their respective checks, traffic is blocked before preparation, waited for during loading, and monitored during execution, completing the configuration. The settings are determined after measuring the actual time it takes for the service to start.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Traffic does not reach unprepared pods
screens.lead: This course content is summarized around the role of three probes.

paragraphs: **startup** waits for slow initialization. Before success, liveness and readiness probes are not executed, and if the process fails, the container terminates and follows its restart policy. This serves as a safeguard for services with long model loading times.

**Liveness** detects and triggers a restart for unrecoverable states. If not carefully configured, it can cause cascading restarts under high load. **Readiness** determines whether the endpoint is ready to receive traffic; if it fails, the endpoint is removed without restarting.

The appropriateness of the configuration is judged starting from the service's startup time. If the startup time is longer than `initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold × periodSeconds`, a startup probe is required.

glossary.def: This is a probe to verify that the slow initialization has completed. No other probe will execute before this one succeeds.
This is a probe that determines whether the container is ready to receive traffic. If it fails, the service endpoint is excluded.
A probe that determines whether a container needs to be restarted.
This value specifies how many consecutive failures are allowed.
The time waited between the container starting and the first probe being executed.

misconceptions.myth: Liveness and readiness can be the same configuration.
misconceptions.fact: If liveness checks fail, the container is restarted; if readiness checks fail, the endpoint is excluded only. Since they produce different outcomes, configure them separately based on the desired behavior.

misconceptions.myth: If responsiveness is slow, extend the liveness interval accordingly.
misconceptions.fact: This value is used for stuck detection after maneuvering and delays detection. A startup probe is appropriate for maneuvering standby.

misconceptions.myth: If readiness fails, the container is restarted.
misconceptions.fact: Readiness failure results in the service endpoint losing the pod's IP address only. The container continues to run unchanged.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: startup determines readiness to commence, liveness determines whether recovery is possible, and readiness determines whether traffic acceptance is possible.
A long-lived service is protected by a startup probe.
Liveness is carefully configured to prevent cascading restarts.
